title: Key-Value Maps and Dictionaries
learningObjectives: Explain a map or dictionary as a collection that associates keys with values.
Retrieve, add, update, and remove entries using keys.
Recognize that keys must be unique within a map and values may repeat.
Describe why key-based lookup differs from positional indexing.
Choose appropriate key types and handle missing-key cases.

understand.concept: A map, dictionary, or associative array stores pairs of keys and values. A key identifies an entry so the program can retrieve or update its associated value. Keys are usually unique, while multiple keys may hold equal values. Different languages use different names, syntax, and key restrictions.
understand.whyItMatters: Key-value structures are useful when data is naturally associated with an identifier, such as a username, product code, setting name, or lookup table. They avoid searching a sequence manually for every matching record, though lookup performance depends on the implementation.
understand.analogy: A dictionary uses a word as a key and its definition as a value. You look up the word rather than asking for the third entry on the page.
understand.analogyLimit: Maps do not all guarantee the same order or lookup complexity. Key equality rules, allowed key types, and missing-key behavior differ by language and implementation.

explain.narrative: Use a map when each entry is identified by a key rather than a position. A map can store a value for each unique key; updating an existing key typically replaces its associated value. Check whether a key exists before relying on a lookup, because some languages return a null-like value while others throw an error or provide an optional result. Choose stable, meaningful keys and avoid assuming values themselves are unique.

examples.title: Create a map
examples.explanation: Each product name is a key associated with a numeric price value.

examples.title: Retrieve by key
examples.explanation: The key 'book' retrieves its associated value, not a value by index position.

examples.title: Add or update a key
examples.explanation: Setting an existing key updates its value; setting a new key adds an entry.

examples.title: Check for a key
examples.explanation: A membership check distinguishes a missing key from a stored value that may be null-like.

examples.title: Remove an entry
examples.explanation: Removing the key deletes its association from the map.

commonMistakes: Assuming map keys can repeat without replacing an earlier association.
Confusing a key with an array index.
Treating a missing key and a stored null-like value as the same without checking.
Assuming all maps preserve insertion order or have identical lookup performance.
